I am 68 years old, and I have worked this land for half a century. With my high-school education, I can read labels and understand what the agronomists say, but at the end of the day I trust what my own eyes have seen across fifty planting seasons. My farm is only six mu — not large, but it is all I have, and with just two of us at home and off-farm work to juggle, I cannot afford crops that demand constant babysitting. Stevia is my crop. It is a reliable cash earner in Quzhou, the buyers know me, and I know exactly how she behaves in our soil.

This spring I will rotary-till the full six mu to break up the clods and make a fine seedbed. Around mid-April I will transplant 8,000 improved stevia seedlings per mu. That density has given me the best leaf yield year after year. For fertility, I will spread 100 jin per mu of general compound fertilizer — 15-15-15 — as a basal dressing before planting. I stopped fussing with separate bags of urea, phosphate and potash long ago; one clean pass with the compound spreader saves labor and the crop responds well to it. That gives me 15 kg of nitrogen, 15 kg of phosphorus and 15 kg of potassium per mu, all in one go.

I have a well, so water is dependable. I will irrigate six times through the season using border irrigation: right after transplanting, then roughly every three to four weeks through the hot summer. Stevia leaves wilt fast if the soil dries out, and our North China Plain summers can turn fierce. For crop protection I will make about eight spray applications in total — insecticides for aphids and leaf-eating caterpillars, one herbicide pass to keep the weeds down, and two or three fungicide sprays when the humidity rises and leaf spot threatens. I often tank-mix the insecticide and fungicide to cut down on trips.

I expect to cut around 600 kg of dried leaf per mu by late August or early September. At the prices the traders have been offering, that should keep the household books in good shape for another year.
